course.title: Introduction to Linguistics
course.description: Linguistics is the scientific study of human language — how it is pronounced, built, arranged, and understood, and how it changes across time and society. This survey tours phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and pragmatics, historical and social variation, acquisition, and writing systems, with concrete examples drawn mostly from English. Topic scope adapted from the Linguistics article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

options: the study of how to speak and write correctly
the scientific study of human language and how it works
the art of translating between languages
questions.explanation: Linguistics describes and explains language as it actually is, rather than prescribing how people ought to speak — see 'What linguistics is'.

questions.prompt: A dictionary editor who records how speakers really use a word, without judging it, is being…
questions.explanation: Describing usage as observed is descriptive; telling people the 'right' form is prescriptive.

questions.prompt: The smallest sound unit that can change the meaning of a word is a…
questions.explanation: Swapping /p/ for /b/ turns 'pat' into 'bat', so /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes — see 'Phonology'.

questions.prompt: The smallest unit of language that carries meaning is a…
questions.explanation: A morpheme is the smallest meaningful piece; 'cats' has two: 'cat' and plural '-s' — see 'Morphology'.

questions.prompt: The branch of linguistics concerned with how words combine into phrases and sentences is…
questions.explanation: Syntax studies sentence structure and what counts as grammatical — see 'Syntax'.

questions.prompt: When someone says 'It's cold in here' to get you to shut the window, the extra message is an example of…
questions.explanation: The literal meaning is about temperature; the intended request is implied — that is pragmatics and implicature.

questions.prompt: Languages that descend from a single common ancestor make up a…
questions.explanation: English, German, and Hindi all belong to the Indo-European family — see 'Language through time and across society'.

lessons.title: What linguistics is: describing, not correcting
lessons.grammar_note: Descriptive linguistics reports how people actually speak; prescriptive rules say how some authority thinks they should. This course is descriptive throughout.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what linguistics studies, tell the difference between a descriptive and a prescriptive statement about language, and name several design features that set human language apart from other signaling systems. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, is a grammar book that bans 'ain't' being descriptive or prescriptive? The goal of this lesson is to shift your stance. Most people meet language only through school rules about what is 'proper'. A linguist instead treats language the way a biologist treats an organism: something to observe, describe, and explain, not something to grade. By the end you should be able to look at a sentence most teachers would red-pen and ask the more interesting question — what system in the speaker's mind produced it, and what regular pattern does it follow?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Linguistics is the scientific study of human language: its sounds, its structure, its meaning, and the way it lives in minds and communities. The field is descriptive, not prescriptive. A descriptive statement reports a pattern that actually occurs — 'many English speakers say I done it'. A prescriptive statement issues a judgment — 'you should say I did it'. Descriptivists note that every variety of a language has its own consistent rules; 'wrong' usually just means 'not the prestige variety'. Linguists also highlight design features that make human language special. Arbitrariness: the sound of a word has no natural link to its meaning (nothing about 'dog' is dog-like). Productivity: a finite set of rules generates an unlimited number of new sentences. Displacement: we can talk about the past, the future, and the imaginary. Duality of patterning: meaningless sounds combine into meaningful units, which recombine into phrases. Cultural transmission: each generation learns language from the last.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Descriptive vs prescriptive. 'Who did you talk to?' — a prescriptivist prefers 'whom' and dislikes ending on a preposition; a descriptivist records that the first version is what fluent speakers overwhelmingly produce, so it is grammatical in that variety. Arbitrariness: a dog is 'dog' in English, 'perro' in Spanish, 'chien' in French — same animal, unrelated sounds, which only works because the pairing is a convention. Productivity: you have never read the sentence 'The purple comet apologized to my grandmother', yet you understand it instantly, because the rules, not a memorized list, build it. Displacement: 'If it rains tomorrow, we'll cancel' refers to an event that has not happened and may never happen — a bee's dance, by contrast, can only report a food source that is there now.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Label each as descriptive (D) or prescriptive (P): (a) 'Never split an infinitive.' (b) 'In casual speech, speakers often split infinitives.' 2) Name the design feature shown by talking about last summer's holiday. 3) Why is the word 'cat' an example of arbitrariness? 4) Give one brand-new grammatical English sentence you are confident no one has written before. 5) Which design feature lets a child invent a sentence they were never taught? Answers: 1) (a) P, (b) D. 2) Displacement — reference to events removed in time. 3) Nothing about the sounds c-a-t resembles the animal; the link is pure convention. 4) Any novel but rule-following sentence counts, e.g. 'My left shoe is writing a symphony.' 5) Productivity (also called creativity or generativity).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming non-standard forms are 'broken' language. Every variety, including regional and social dialects, is rule-governed; 'standard' is the variety that happens to carry social prestige, not the only logical one. Mistake: confusing arbitrariness with randomness — within a community the sound-meaning pairing is fixed and shared, it is just not derivable from the meaning. Mistake: thinking displacement is rare; almost every ordinary conversation uses it. Exit: (a) Rewrite 'You must never say gonna' as a descriptive observation. (b) Which feature explains why you can understand a sentence you have never heard? Answers: (a) 'Many speakers say gonna in casual registers.' (b) Productivity.

lessons.title: Phonetics: the sounds of speech
lessons.grammar_note: The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) gives each speech sound one symbol. Because true IPA symbols cannot all be shown in plain text here, this course writes them as ASCII approximations in brackets, and says so wherever it does.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how speech sounds are made in the mouth using three dimensions — voicing, place of articulation, and manner of articulation — and read the ASCII phonetic notation this course uses. Warm-up: put your fingers on your throat and say a long 'zzzz', then 'ssss'. One buzzes and one does not — why? Phonetics is the study of the physical speech signal: how sounds are produced (articulatory phonetics), how they travel as sound waves (acoustic phonetics), and how they are heard. We focus on articulation, because it gives you a vocabulary for describing any sound in any language. A note on symbols: linguists use the International Phonetic Alphabet, where one symbol always maps to one sound. Many IPA characters are special and cannot be typed in plain ASCII, so throughout this course they are approximated — for example the 'th' in 'thin' is written [th] and the vowel in 'bit' as [ih]. These are stand-ins, not official IPA.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: English spelling is a poor guide to sound: 'ough' is pronounced differently in 'though', 'through', 'cough', and 'rough'. Phonetics fixes this by describing the actual articulation. Every consonant can be pinned down by three questions. Voicing: are the vocal folds vibrating? [z] is voiced, [s] is voiceless — the buzz you felt. Place of articulation: where in the vocal tract is the airflow obstructed? Lips together give bilabials [p b m]; tongue tip at the ridge behind the teeth gives alveolars [t d n s z]; the back of the tongue at the soft palate gives velars [k g]. Manner of articulation: how is the air obstructed? A full stop then release is a plosive [p t k]; a narrow channel causing friction is a fricative [f s sh]; lowering the velum to route air through the nose gives a nasal [m n ng]. Vowels are described instead by tongue height, backness, and lip rounding.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Full descriptions (symbols are ASCII approximations). [p] as in 'pat': voiceless bilabial plosive — vocal folds still, lips closed then popped open. [b] as in 'bat': same but voiced; [p] and [b] differ only in voicing. [m] as in 'mat': voiced bilabial nasal — lips closed, air through the nose. [s] as in 'sip': voiceless alveolar fricative. [z] as in 'zip': voiced alveolar fricative — the buzz from the warm-up. [k] as in 'kit': voiceless velar plosive. Vowels: 'beat' has a high front unrounded vowel [ee]; 'boot' has a high back rounded vowel [oo]; say them in turn and feel your tongue slide back and your lips round. 'Father' has a low back vowel [ah]. Notice that 'c' spells [k] in 'cat' but [s] in 'city' — one letter, two sounds, which is exactly why phoneticians prefer one-symbol-per-sound notation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is [g] (as in 'go') voiced or voiceless? 2) Name the place of articulation shared by [t], [d], and [n]. 3) What manner of articulation does [f] (as in 'fan') have? 4) Which two of [p], [b], [m] are plosives? 5) Give the three-part description of [t] in 'top'. 6) How many distinct speech sounds are in the word 'cat', and what are they? Answers: 1) Voiced. 2) Alveolar (tongue tip at the ridge behind the upper teeth). 3) Fricative (friction between lower lip and upper teeth, a labiodental fricative). 4) [p] and [b]; [m] is a nasal. 5) Voiceless alveolar plosive. 6) Three: [k] + [ah] + [t], even though it is spelled with three letters that happen to match this time.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: counting letters instead of sounds — 'thought' has seven letters but only three sounds, roughly [th] + [aw] + [t]. Mistake: assuming voiced and voiceless sounds feel totally different; often they share place and manner and differ only in the vocal-fold buzz ([s]/[z], [p]/[b], [t]/[d], [k]/[g]). Mistake: treating these ASCII tags as real IPA — they are readable approximations only. Exit: (a) Give the voiced partner of [t]. (b) State the manner of articulation of [n]. (c) True or false: the number of letters always equals the number of sounds. Answers: (a) [d]. (b) Nasal. (c) False — spelling and sound diverge constantly in English.

lessons.title: Phonology: the system behind the sounds
lessons.grammar_note: A phoneme is a sound that distinguishes meaning; an allophone is one of its predictable context-dependent variants. Phonemes are written in /slashes/, allophones in [brackets]; symbols below are ASCII approximations.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell phonemes from allophones, use minimal pairs to prove two sounds are separate phonemes, and state a simple phonological rule in words. Warm-up: say 'pin' and 'spin' with a slip of paper in front of your lips. The paper jumps on 'pin' but barely moves on 'spin'. Same letter 'p' — what changed? Where phonetics describes raw sounds, phonology studies the sound system of a particular language: which differences matter, which do not, and what patterns govern the variation. Every language draws the lines in its own place, which is why the 'same' sound can be a meaningful contrast in one language and an ignorable detail in another.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A phoneme is a sound category that can distinguish words in a language. An allophone is a predictable variant of a phoneme that appears in a particular context and never changes meaning. The puff of air on the 'p' of 'pin' is aspiration, written [p-h]; the 'p' of 'spin' is unaspirated [p]. English speakers hear both as the same /p/ — the difference is allophonic, fully predictable from position, so it never distinguishes two words. The test for separate phonemes is the minimal pair: two words that differ in exactly one sound and mean different things. 'pat' vs 'bat' differ only in /p/ vs /b/ and mean different things, proving /p/ and /b/ are distinct phonemes. Allophones, by contrast, occur in complementary distribution: each shows up only in its own environment, so swapping them yields a foreign accent, never a new word.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Minimal pairs. 'bit' vs 'bet' isolates the vowels /ih/ vs /eh/ as distinct phonemes. 'sip' vs 'zip' isolates /s/ vs /z/. 'cat' vs 'cap' isolates final /t/ vs /p/. Allophonic rule. English voiceless plosives are aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable and plain after /s/: /p/ is [p-h] in 'pin' but [p] in 'spin'. A learner who aspirates the 'p' in 'spin' sounds slightly off but is still understood — the choice carries no meaning. The English plural adds another clean rule: write it /s/ after a voiceless sound ('cats' = [kats]), /z/ after a voiced sound ('dogs' = [dogz]), and [uh-z] after a hiss ('buses'). You already obey this rule without being taught it — evidence that phonology is unconscious knowledge, not a school lesson.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Do 'ship' and 'shop' form a minimal pair? What sounds do they isolate? 2) Is the aspiration difference between 'top' and 'stop' phonemic or allophonic in English? 3) Give the plural ending sound for 'books', 'beds', and 'churches'. 4) Find a minimal pair proving /m/ and /n/ are separate English phonemes. 5) Two sounds in complementary distribution are allophones of — what? Answers: 1) Yes; it isolates the vowels /ih/ vs /ah-type/ (bit-class vs hot-class). 2) Allophonic — predictable from position, no meaning change. 3) 'books' = /s/, 'beds' = /z/, 'churches' = [uh-z]. 4) e.g. 'map' vs 'nap', or 'sum' vs 'sun'. 5) One and the same phoneme.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming one letter equals one phoneme — the letter 'x' in 'box' spells two phonemes /k/ + /s/. Mistake: thinking a sound that is a separate phoneme in English must be one in every language; aspirated and unaspirated plosives are distinct phonemes in Hindi, where they do distinguish words, even though English treats them as one. Mistake: calling any two different sounds a minimal pair — the words must differ in exactly one sound and have different meanings. Exit: (a) What does a minimal pair prove? (b) Is the 'p' puff in 'pin' versus 'spin' meaningful in English? Answers: (a) That the two swapped sounds are separate phonemes. (b) No — it is allophonic and predictable, so it carries no meaning.

lessons.title: Morphology: how words are built
lessons.grammar_note: A morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit. Free morphemes can stand alone ('cat'); bound morphemes cannot ('-s', 're-', '-ness') and must attach to something.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Break words into morphemes, tell free from bound morphemes and roots from affixes, and distinguish derivation (making new words) from inflection (marking grammar). Warm-up: how many meaningful pieces are in 'unhappiness'? List them. Morphology studies word structure — the internal architecture of words. Just as sentences are built from words, words are built from smaller meaningful bricks. Knowing these bricks explains how speakers coax new words out of old ones and why a word you have never seen, like 'de-friend-ed', is instantly interpretable.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A morpheme is the smallest unit that carries meaning or grammatical function. 'Cats' has two: the free morpheme 'cat' (can stand alone) and the bound morpheme '-s' (must attach). A root is the core that carries the central meaning; affixes attach to it — prefixes before ('re-do'), suffixes after ('quick-ly'). Two big jobs divide the affixes. Derivation creates a new word, often changing its part of speech: 'happy' (adjective) plus '-ness' gives 'happiness' (noun); 'teach' plus '-er' gives 'teacher'. Inflection does not make a new word; it marks a grammatical feature on the same word: plural '-s', past tense '-ed', comparative '-er' on adjectives. English has only a handful of inflections; many languages have far more. Other word-formation processes: compounding joins free morphemes ('tooth' + 'brush' = 'toothbrush'); blending fuses parts ('breakfast' + 'lunch' = 'brunch'); acronyms read initials ('radar'); clipping shortens ('advertisement' to 'ad').

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Full parse. 'unhappiness' = un- (prefix, 'not') + happy (root) + -ness (suffix, 'state of'): three morphemes, two of them bound. 'rewrites' = re- (prefix, 'again') + write (root) + -s (inflection, present tense third person): the first is derivational, the last inflectional. 'teachers' = teach (root) + -er (derivational, 'one who') + -s (inflectional, plural); note the order — derivation sits closer to the root than inflection. Word formation: 'smog' is a blend of 'smoke' and 'fog'; 'brunch' blends 'breakfast' and 'lunch'; 'laptop' is a compound; 'NASA' is an acronym; 'gym' is a clipping of 'gymnasium'. Cross-linguistic note: Turkish can pile many morphemes into one word, so a single Turkish word may translate a whole English sentence — a pattern called agglutination.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Break 'disagreements' into morphemes and label each. 2) Is '-ed' in 'walked' derivational or inflectional? 3) Name the word-formation process behind 'motel' (motor + hotel). 4) Which morpheme in 'teacher' is free? 5) Give the root of 'unbelievable'. 6) Is 'cats' one word made of how many morphemes? Answers: 1) dis- (prefix, 'not') + agree (root) + -ment (derivational, makes a noun) + -s (inflectional, plural) = four morphemes. 2) Inflectional — it marks past tense without making a new word. 3) Blending. 4) 'teach' (the root); '-er' is bound. 5) 'believe' (un- and -able are affixes). 6) Two: 'cat' + plural '-s'.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: equating morphemes with syllables — 'crocodile' has three syllables but is a single morpheme, while 'dogs' has one syllable but two morphemes. Mistake: confusing derivation and inflection; a quick test is that derivation can change the part of speech and often blocks further inflection inside it, whereas inflection sits at the outer edge. Mistake: assuming every word has multiple morphemes — many common words ('tree', 'run', 'and') are single free morphemes. Exit: (a) How many morphemes in 'reheated'? (b) Does '-ness' derive or inflect? Answers: (a) Three: re- + heat + -ed. (b) It derives — it turns an adjective into a noun.

questions.prompt: A statement reporting how people actually speak, without judging it, is…
questions.explanation: Describing observed usage is descriptive; issuing a 'should' is prescriptive.

questions.prompt: The ability to talk about events in the past or future is the design feature called…
questions.explanation: Displacement is reference to things removed in time or space, or imaginary.

questions.prompt: Describing [s] as a 'voiceless alveolar fricative' uses which three dimensions of articulation?
questions.explanation: Consonants are pinned down by voicing, place, and manner of articulation.

questions.prompt: The pair 'pat' and 'bat' is a minimal pair that proves…
questions.explanation: Changing exactly one sound changes the meaning, so /p/ and /b/ are distinct phonemes.

questions.prompt: The aspirated 'p' of 'pin' versus the plain 'p' of 'spin' is, in English, an example of…
questions.explanation: The variation is predictable from context and never changes meaning, so these are allophones of /p/.
'-ness' is a derivational suffix that turns the adjective 'happy' into a noun.

questions.prompt: How many morphemes are in the word 'cats'?

lessons.title: Syntax: how phrases combine
lessons.grammar_note: Grammaticality is about structure, not meaning or politeness. 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' is grammatical but meaningless; 'Furiously sleep ideas green colorless' is neither.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: See sentences as nested phrases rather than flat strings of words, identify constituents, read a simple phrase-structure tree, and judge grammaticality. Warm-up: in 'The old dog chased the cat', which three words group together most tightly? Syntax studies how words combine into phrases and phrases into sentences, and what makes a string well-formed. A key insight is that sentences are not beads on a line; they are built in hierarchical layers. Groups of words called constituents behave as units, and the rules operate on those units, which is why a sentence of modest length can still be unlimited in the structures it allows.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Words cluster into constituents — phrases that act as single units. A noun phrase (NP) such as 'the old dog' can be replaced by a single pronoun ('it'), moved, or questioned as a whole: that substitution test reveals the constituent. A verb phrase (VP) such as 'chased the cat' combines a verb with its objects. A sentence (S) typically pairs an NP subject with a VP predicate: S then NP plus VP. These relationships are drawn as a phrase-structure tree, where branches show which words group under which phrase. Grammaticality — whether a string obeys the rules of the language — is independent of meaning: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' is perfectly grammatical yet nonsensical, while word salad like 'sleep green furiously ideas colorless' is ungrammatical though built from the same words. Structure also creates ambiguity: one string of words can correspond to two different trees, and therefore two meanings.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Constituency. In 'The old dog chased the cat', 'the old dog' is an NP (replace it with 'it': 'It chased the cat'), and 'chased the cat' is a VP. A rough tree: S branches into NP ['the old dog'] and VP ['chased' + NP 'the cat']. Structural ambiguity. 'I saw the man with the telescope' has two trees: in one, 'with the telescope' attaches to the VP (I used the telescope to see him); in the other, it attaches to the NP 'the man' (the man who had the telescope). Same words, two structures, two meanings. Movement. The question 'What did you see?' is understood as if 'what' started as the object of 'see' and moved to the front — evidence that syntax manipulates whole constituents, not isolated words. Recursion lets this nest without limit: 'the cat the dog chased ran', and you can keep embedding.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In 'My neighbor planted tall sunflowers', name the subject NP and the VP. 2) Is 'Sincerity admires the table' grammatical, meaningful, both, or neither? 3) Give the two readings of 'She fed her the dog food' — or of any ambiguous phrase you prefer. 4) What single pronoun can replace 'the big red bus'? 5) True or false: a grammatical sentence must make sense. Answers: 1) Subject NP 'my neighbor'; VP 'planted tall sunflowers'. 2) Grammatical but not meaningful — the structure is fine, the semantics is odd. 3) Reading A: she fed dog food to her; reading B: she fed her to the dog, as food. 4) 'it'. 5) False — grammaticality is structural and independent of sense.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: equating grammaticality with making sense or sounding polite — they are separate dimensions. Mistake: treating a sentence as a flat list; missing the hierarchy makes attachment ambiguities look like single meanings. Mistake: thinking long sentences need new rules — recursion reuses the same rules to embed phrases inside phrases. Exit: (a) What test shows that 'the old dog' is a single constituent? (b) Give a sentence that is grammatical but meaningless. Answers: (a) Substitution — you can replace the whole group with the pronoun 'it'. (b) 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' (or any well-formed but nonsensical string).

lessons.title: Semantics and pragmatics: meaning and implicature
lessons.grammar_note: Semantics is literal, context-free meaning; pragmatics is meaning in use, filled in by context. 'Can you pass the salt?' is a question by semantics but a request by pragmatics.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Separate literal meaning (semantics) from meaning-in-context (pragmatics), recognize entailment, and explain conversational implicature using Grice's cooperative principle. Warm-up: a friend asks 'Did you like the film?' and you answer 'Well, the popcorn was good.' What have you communicated without saying it? Semantics studies the stable, literal meaning of words and sentences; pragmatics studies how speakers mean more than they literally say, and how listeners recover that extra content from context. Together they explain why conversation works even though we almost never spell everything out.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: On the semantic side, meaning has layers. Sense is a word's inherent content; reference is the thing it points to on an occasion ('the president' refers to different people over time). Entailment is a meaning relation where one sentence's truth guarantees another's: 'The dog barked loudly' entails 'The dog barked.' On the pragmatic side, Grice proposed that conversation is cooperative, governed by maxims: be truthful (quality), as informative as needed but no more (quantity), relevant (relation), and clear (manner). When a speaker seems to flout a maxim, the listener infers an unstated meaning — a conversational implicature. Saying 'the popcorn was good' when asked about the film flouts quantity (you said less than expected about the film), implicating that you did not like it. Pragmatics also covers presupposition (background taken for granted — 'Have you stopped smoking?' presupposes you once smoked) and deixis (words like 'here', 'now', 'you' whose meaning depends on the speech situation).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Entailment: 'She adopted two kittens' entails 'She adopted at least one animal'; if the first is true the second must be. Implicature via quantity: a reference letter that says only 'This candidate has excellent handwriting' implicates that there is little else to praise, because a cooperative writer would have said more if they could. Implicature via relation: 'A: I'm out of gas. B: There's a station around the corner.' B's relevance implies the station is open and sells gas. Indirect speech act: 'Can you pass the salt?' is semantically a yes/no question about ability, but pragmatically a polite request — answering only 'Yes' while doing nothing is a joke precisely because it ignores the pragmatics. Presupposition survives negation: both 'The king of France is bald' and 'The king of France is not bald' presuppose that such a king exists.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Does 'Tom ran a marathon' entail 'Tom ran'? 2) Which Gricean maxim is flouted by answering 'Some of the guests have arrived' when in fact all have, implicating 'not all'? 3) What does 'Have you stopped texting in class?' presuppose? 4) Name one deictic word in 'Meet me here tomorrow.' 5) Is 'Can you reach the top shelf?' literally a question or a request? Answers: 1) Yes — the first guarantees the second. 2) Quantity — the speaker gives less information than available, implicating that not all arrived. 3) That you used to text in class. 4) 'me', 'here', or 'tomorrow' (all depend on who speaks, where, and when). 5) Literally (semantically) a question about ability; pragmatically, usually a request.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating implicature as part of literal meaning — an implicature can be cancelled ('The popcorn was good — and honestly, so was the whole film'), whereas an entailment cannot. Mistake: confusing entailment with presupposition; presuppositions survive negation and questioning, entailments do not. Mistake: assuming the literal form of a sentence equals its communicative force; questions can be requests, and statements can be warnings. Exit: (a) Give the implicature of 'Some students passed.' (b) Is 'The dog barked loudly' entailing 'The dog barked'? Answers: (a) That not all students passed (a quantity implicature). (b) Yes — a clear entailment.

lessons.title: Language through time and across society
lessons.grammar_note: Change and variation are not decay. Sound change is regular, and every dialect and register is a complete, rule-governed system — differences track history and social context, not correctness.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how languages change and split into families, outline the comparative method that reconstructs ancestors, and describe how language varies across regions and social situations through dialects and registers. Warm-up: English 'father', German 'Vater', Latin 'pater', Sanskrit 'pitar' all mean the same and start with similar sounds — coincidence, or clue? This lesson joins two kinds of variation: historical (how language differs across time) and social (how it differs across communities and situations). Both show that variation is the normal, systematic state of language, not a flaw in it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Languages change constantly — in pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar — and when a community splits, its varieties drift apart until they become separate languages. Languages descended from one ancestor form a language family; English, German, Latin, Greek, Persian, and Hindi all belong to Indo-European. Historical linguists reconstruct unrecorded ancestors with the comparative method: they line up cognates (words of common origin) across related languages, find regular sound correspondences, and infer the earlier form. The regularity is key — sound change applies across the board, as captured by Grimm's Law, which relates Latin 'p' to English 'f' (pater/father, pes/foot). On the social side, sociolinguistics studies variation within a living community. A dialect is a regional or social variety with its own consistent pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar; a register is the style a speaker selects for a situation (formal, casual, technical). Studies of variables — such as whether speakers pronounce 'r' after a vowel — show that variation correlates systematically with region, class, age, and context, and that one variety's prestige is social, not linguistic.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Cognates and correspondence: Latin 'pater', 'piscis', 'pes' line up with English 'father', 'fish', 'foot' — Latin 'p' corresponds to English 'f' every time, a regular correspondence that reconstructs an Indo-European parent with an original 'p'. Borrowing vs inheritance: English 'beef' (from French) and 'cow' (inherited Germanic) show how the Norman Conquest layered French vocabulary onto English. Semantic change: 'nice' once meant 'foolish', then 'precise', now 'pleasant'. Social variation: in classic sociolinguistic fieldwork, New York speakers pronounced post-vowel 'r' more often in careful speech and in higher-status settings than in casual speech — the same person varies by register. Dialect grammar: 'I haven't done anything' and 'I ain't done nothing' follow different but equally regular rules; the double negative is systematic in many English dialects and standard in languages like Spanish ('no he hecho nada').

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What do we call words in different languages that descend from the same source? 2) Latin 'pisces' and English 'fish' illustrate which regular correspondence? 3) Is switching from 'Hello, how may I help you?' to 'Hey, what's up?' a change of dialect or register? 4) Name the language family English and Hindi share. 5) Give one example of semantic change. Answers: 1) Cognates. 2) Latin 'p' corresponds to English 'f' (part of Grimm's Law). 3) Register — same speaker, different situation and style. 4) Indo-European. 5) 'nice' shifting from 'foolish' to 'pleasant' (or 'gay', 'awful', etc.).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling language change 'corruption' — change is constant, regular, and produces new systems that are neither better nor worse than the old. Mistake: treating cognates and loanwords as the same; cognates are inherited from a shared ancestor, loanwords are borrowed later. Mistake: ranking dialects as 'good' or 'bad'; the prestige of a variety reflects its speakers' social power, not its linguistic quality. Exit: (a) Which method reconstructs an unrecorded parent language? (b) Is a formal versus casual style difference a matter of dialect or register? Answers: (a) The comparative method. (b) Register.

lessons.title: Language in the mind and on the page
lessons.grammar_note: Children acquire their first language in a regular sequence without explicit teaching; writing, by contrast, is a comparatively recent invention and is taught. Speech is primary, writing secondary.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the stages of first-language acquisition and a few findings of psycholinguistics, then classify the world's writing systems by what their symbols stand for. Warm-up: a three-year-old says 'I goed to the park.' That is a mistake, yet it reveals something impressive about the child's mind — what? This closing lesson looks at language in two places it lives beyond grammar books: in the developing and processing mind (acquisition and psycholinguistics) and in the visible medium of script (writing systems). Both reinforce a theme of the course — that language is an unconscious, rule-governed system that speakers build and use without studying it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: First-language acquisition unfolds in a predictable order with little explicit teaching: cooing, then babbling, a one-word stage around age one, two-word combinations near two, then rapid grammatical growth. A famous clue is overregularization — a child who said 'went' earlier starts saying 'goed', applying the regular '-ed' rule to an irregular verb. The error proves the child has induced a rule, not just memorized words. Many researchers propose a critical period: language is acquired most easily in early childhood. Psycholinguistics studies real-time processing — how we retrieve words (lexical access) and parse sentences. Garden-path sentences like 'The horse raced past the barn fell' briefly mislead the parser, exposing how it builds structure on the fly. Writing systems, finally, are classified by what each symbol represents: a logographic system uses a symbol per word or morpheme (Chinese characters); a syllabic system (syllabary) uses a symbol per syllable (Japanese kana); an alphabet uses symbols for consonants and vowels (Latin, Greek); an abjad marks mainly consonants (Arabic, Hebrew); an abugida marks consonant-vowel units (Devanagari).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Acquisition sequence: babbling ('bababa') around six months; first words ('mama', 'dog') near one year; two-word utterances ('more milk', 'daddy go') around two; then explosive growth. Overregularization: 'foots' for 'feet', 'runned' for 'ran' — the child over-applies a real rule, evidence of rule-learning, and these errors fade as exceptions are relearned. Processing: in 'The old man the boats', readers stumble because they first read 'man' as a noun before reinterpreting it as a verb ('to man'). Writing systems: the English alphabet maps letters to sounds (imperfectly); Chinese writing is largely logographic, so speakers of different Chinese varieties can share characters while pronouncing them differently; Japanese combines logographic kanji with two syllabaries; Arabic script is an abjad, writing consonants and leaving most short vowels to the reader.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why does a child saying 'goed' show rule-learning rather than failure? 2) What is a system with one symbol per syllable called? 3) Name the processing phenomenon in 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' 4) Which writing-system type marks mainly consonants? 5) Does acquisition normally require formal teaching? Answers: 1) The child has generalized the regular past-tense '-ed' rule and over-applied it to an irregular verb, which only makes sense if a rule was learned. 2) A syllabary (a syllabic system). 3) A garden-path sentence (temporary misparse). 4) An abjad (e.g. Arabic, Hebrew). 5) No — first-language acquisition happens through exposure, without explicit instruction.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading children's errors as sloppiness — overregularizations are a sign of active rule induction and are a healthy stage. Mistake: thinking writing is just speech written down; writing is a separate, invented technology, and many languages have none. Mistake: assuming every script is an alphabet; logographies, syllabaries, abjads, and abugidas all work differently. Exit: (a) What does overregularization ('goed') reveal about a child's mind? (b) Classify the Latin script used for English. Answers: (a) That the child has internalized a grammatical rule and is generalizing it. (b) An alphabet — symbols stand for individual consonant and vowel sounds.
